name: GABA-A Receptor
baseline: Tonic inhibitory tone, gates CNS firing, anxiolysis, muscle relaxation, slow-wave sleep.
mech: Ligand binding opens a pentameric Cl⁻ channel; anion influx hyperpolarizes the membrane and raises the action-potential threshold, damping excitation.
stahl: Stahl frames GABA-A positive allosteric modulation (benzodiazepines, “Z-drugs,” barbiturates) as the core of anxiolytic/hypnotic therapy; abrupt withdrawal removes tonic inhibition and precipitates seizures.

name: NMDA Glutamate Receptor
baseline: Excitatory plasticity, long-term potentiation, learning, memory consolidation.
mech: Needs glutamate + glycine co-binding and depolarization to expel the Mg²⁺ pore block, then admits Ca²⁺ and Na⁺ to drive synaptic strengthening.
stahl: Stahl describes NMDA hypofunction as a leading model of schizophrenia’s negative/cognitive symptoms; therapeutic blockade is harnessed by ketamine/esketamine (rapid antidepressant) and memantine (neuroprotection).
over: Excitotoxic neuronal death (stroke, TBI, status epilepticus)

name: Dopamine D2 Receptor
baseline: Motor and reward equilibrium, striatal gating, mesolimbic salience, prolactin suppression.
mech: Gi/o inhibits adenylyl cyclase (↓ cAMP) and opens GIRK K⁺ channels, damping postsynaptic excitability across striatal and limbic circuits.
stahl: Stahl: mesolimbic D2 hyperactivity drives positive psychotic symptoms; D2 antagonism/partial agonism is the shared antipsychotic & antimanic mechanism, with nigrostriatal blockade producing EPS and tardive dyskinesia.
over: Aberrant salience: ideas of reference, paranoid delusion
Impulse control disorder on dopamine agonists: gambling, hypersexuality, binge eating
Chorea and dyskinesia at high dopaminergic load
under: Acute dystonia: oculogyric crisis, torticollis, laryngospasm
Akathisia: inner restlessness, inability to remain seated
Tardive dyskinesia: orofacial and limb choreoathetosis
Neuroleptic malignant syndrome: rigidity, hyperthermia, autonomic instability

name: Dopamine D1 Receptor
baseline: Prefrontal cognition & working memory; excitatory “direct pathway” for movement initiation.
mech: Gs activates adenylyl cyclase (↑cAMP → PKA). Stahl notes D1 is the dominant cortical dopamine receptor, tuning the signal-to-noise of prefrontal pyramidal networks.
stahl: Stahl emphasizes the prefrontal D1 “inverted-U”: too little OR too much D1 tone degrades cognition. Optimizing D1 signaling underlies the pro-cognitive aim of stimulant and noradrenergic ADHD therapy.
over: Dyskinesia in the direct motor pathway

name: DAT, Dopamine Transporter
baseline: Clears synaptic dopamine, terminates signaling, recycles transmitter, sets reward & motor tone.
mech: Na⁺/Cl⁻-dependent presynaptic reuptake. A transporter, not a receptor: blockade raises synaptic dopamine; “overstimulated/understimulated” denotes synaptic dopamine excess vs. deficit.
stahl: Stahl (Table 2-5): methylphenidate and amphetamine act indirectly by inhibiting/reversing DAT, raising dopamine to improve ADHD, depression, and wakefulness, the therapeutic mirror of cocaine’s abuse liability.

name: Serotonin 5-HT2A
baseline: Cortical cognitive modulation, gates glutamate release, cognitive flexibility, cranial vascular tone.
mech: Gq activates phospholipase C → IP3/DAG → intracellular Ca²⁺ release and PKC activation in cortical pyramidal networks.
stahl: Stahl: 5-HT2A antagonism defines the “atypical” antipsychotic advantage, it disinhibits nigrostriatal dopamine (reducing EPS) and tempers cortical glutamate, easing positive symptoms.
under: Normalized striatal dopamine → lower EPS risk

name: Serotonin 5-HT1A
baseline: Somatodendritic autoreceptor + postsynaptic limbic receptor, sets serotonergic tone, anxiolysis, mood.
mech: Gi/o lowers cAMP and opens GIRK K⁺ channels. Presynaptic raphe autoreceptors slow 5-HT firing; their desensitization underlies the delayed onset of SSRI benefit (Stahl).
stahl: Stahl (Table 2-4): 5-HT1A partial agonism is anxiolytic, reduces parkinsonism, and boosts SSRI/SNRI antidepressant action, the mechanism shared by buspirone and the “pines/pips” with 5-HT1A pharmacology.
over: At excess: sedation, contribution to serotonin syndrome

name: Serotonin 5-HT2C
baseline: Inhibits downstream dopamine/norepinephrine release; regulates appetite, mood, and prolactin.
mech: Gq → PLC → Ca²⁺/PKC. Net inhibitory on mesocortical DA/NE. Stahl notes 5-HT2C antagonism disinhibits DA/NE in cortex, contributing to antidepressant effect.
stahl: Stahl (Table 2-4): 5-HT2C antagonism is antidepressant (disinhibits prefrontal DA/NE), but the same blockade drives the weight gain seen with agents like mirtazapine and olanzapine.

name: SERT, Serotonin Transporter
baseline: Clears synaptic serotonin, stable mood, sleep architecture, appetite, low rumination.
mech: Na⁺/Cl⁻-dependent presynaptic reuptake. A transporter, not a receptor: SSRIs/SNRIs block it to raise synaptic 5-HT. States denote synaptic serotonin excess vs. deficit.
stahl: Stahl (Table 2-5): SERT inhibition by SSRIs/SNRIs is the foundational antidepressant/anxiolytic mechanism; the 5-HTTLPR short allele confers stress-linked mood vulnerability.

name: Beta-1 (β1) Adrenergic
baseline: Cardiorespiratory drive, heart rate, contractility, AV conduction, renin release.
mech: Gs → adenylyl cyclase → cAMP → PKA phosphorylates L-type Ca²⁺ channels, increasing cardiac rate and force.
stahl: Stahl notes peripheral β1 effects are mostly off-target in psychiatry; centrally, lipophilic propranolol blunts the somatic (tremor, palpitations) symptoms of performance anxiety and adrenergic hyperarousal.

name: Alpha-1 Adrenergic
baseline: Vascular tone & smooth-muscle contraction, blood pressure, postural response, sphincter/pupil tone.
mech: Gq → PLC → IP3/DAG → ↑Ca²⁺ → smooth-muscle contraction, raising peripheral resistance and blood pressure.
stahl: Stahl (Table 2-4): α1 antagonism improves PTSD nightmares (prazosin) and Alzheimer agitation, but the same blockade by many antipsychotics causes orthostatic hypotension and sedation.

name: Alpha-2 Adrenergic
baseline: Presynaptic autoinhibition of NE release, calm arousal, stable BP, attention, fear extinction.
mech: Gi/o inhibits adenylyl cyclase. Presynaptic α2A autoreceptors give negative feedback on NE; central activation lowers sympathetic outflow and blood pressure.
stahl: Stahl (Table 2-4): postsynaptic α2A agonism (guanfacine, clonidine) strengthens prefrontal connectivity, improving ADHD attention and behavioral control; α2 antagonism (mirtazapine) disinhibits NE & 5-HT for antidepressant effect.
over: On abrupt withdrawal: rebound hypertension, tremor
Risk of ACS/stroke from BP surge

name: NET, Norepinephrine Transporter
baseline: Clears synaptic NE, focused attention, working memory, controlled anxiety, pain modulation.
mech: Na⁺/Cl⁻-dependent reuptake (noradrenergic analogue of SERT). Inhibitors raise synaptic NE. States denote synaptic NE excess vs. deficit.
stahl: Stahl (Table 2-5): NET inhibition (atomoxetine, reboxetine, SNRIs, TCAs) raises NE to treat ADHD, depression, and neuropathic pain; in prefrontal cortex NET also clears dopamine, reinforcing the pro-attention effect.
over: ACS / stroke risk in vulnerable patients

name: M1 Muscarinic
baseline: Postsynaptic cognition & striatal balance, memory, learning, reciprocal control with dopamine.
mech: Gq → PLC → IP3/DAG excitation. Stahl: M1 sits in reciprocal balance with striatal D2, D2 blockade disinhibits ACh, and M1 antagonism then restores motor balance.
stahl: Stahl (Table 2-4 & Ch. 5): M1 agonism is procognitive/antipsychotic (the basis of xanomeline-trospium); M1 antagonism reduces drug-induced parkinsonism but at the cost of the classic anticholinergic burden, sedation, memory loss, and peripheral dryness.
under: Dry mouth, blurred vision, constipation, urinary retention

name: Histamine H1
baseline: Wakefulness & arousal, promotes alert waking state, appetite regulation, cortical activation.
mech: Gq → PLC excitation in cortex and tuberomammillary arousal pathways. CNS H1 blockade lowers histaminergic wake drive (Stahl).
stahl: Stahl (Table 2-4): H1 antagonism is therapeutic for anxiety and insomnia, but the same central blockade produces the sedation and weight gain that limit many antidepressants and antipsychotics (e.g., mirtazapine, olanzapine, quetiapine).
under: Weight gain and increased appetite (also sedation-driven inactivity, metabolic effects)

name: μ-Opioid Receptor (MOR)
baseline: Nociceptive gating, modulates pain transmission, descending inhibition, satiety, gut motility.
mech: Gi/o inhibits adenylyl cyclase (↓cAMP); βγ opens GIRK K⁺ channels and closes Ca²⁺ channels to block nociceptive transmitter release.
stahl: Stahl frames MOR within reward and dependence circuitry; partial agonism (buprenorphine) and antagonism (naltrexone) anchor addiction maintenance, while naloxone reverses acute overdose at the brainstem.
